MUJAHID:v1p308#5/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p308#5/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p308#5/r1.claim: Mujahid says the evening portion of night is an hour at the night prayer, al-isha.

MUQATIL:11:114/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:11:114/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:11:114/r1.claim: The prayers at the two ends of the day are dawn, al-ula, and afternoon; the night prayers are sunset and evening.

MUQATIL:11:114/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:11:114/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:11:114/r2.claim: The five prayers erase sins provided major sins are avoided; this was revealed about Abu Miqbal, also named Amir b. Qays al-Ansari of Banu al-Najjar.

MUQATIL:11:114/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:11:114/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:11:114/r3.claim: Abu Miqbal confessed to the Prophet that he had made advances to a woman but had not had intercourse; the obligatory prayer he prayed with the Prophet expiated it.

MUQATIL:11:114/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:11:114/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:11:114/r4.claim: The verse's prayer reminder echoes God's command to Moses to establish prayer for remembrance in 20:14.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p292/r5.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p292/r5.speaker: الحسن
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p292/r5.claim: Al-Hasan says the two ends of the day run from the dawn prayer to the afternoon prayer.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p294/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p294/r1.speaker: قتادة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p294/r1.claim: Qatāda identifies the ends of the day as dawn and afternoon prayers, and the near parts of night as Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r1.claim: Ibn Masud recounts a man who struck a woman on her backside and asked the Prophet about expiation; after asking whether intercourse occurred, the Prophet waited for revelation, and this verse came down.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r2.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r2.claim: Qatada identifies the two ends of the day as dawn and afternoon prayers, and the night approaches as Maghrib and Isha.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r3.speaker: مجاهد
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r3.claim: Mujahid likewise identifies dawn, afternoon, Maghrib, and Isha; he explains the good deeds that erase sins as the prayers.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas explains both the erasing good deeds and the remaining righteous deeds as the five prayers.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p313#3/r5.claim: A man confessed to kissing and fondling a woman without intercourse; the Prophet recited this passage, and, answering Muadh, said its lesson applies to everyone.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p315/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p315/r1.speaker: يحيى بن جعدة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p315/r1.claim: A Companion found a woman by a pool, stopped after an arousal, repented to the Prophet, and was told to seek forgiveness and pray four units; the Prophet then recited the verse.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p315/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p315/r2.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p315/r2.claim: A rigorous worshiper who made people despair of God's mercy was told after death that he deserved Hell and would now be made to despair of mercy.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p315/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p315/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p315/r3.claim: The Prophet said a mother bird entrusted herself and her chick to people out of mercy for her young, and God's mercy toward the believing servant is greater.

AKHFASH:v1p391/r3.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p391/r3.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p391/r3.claim: The yāʾ in طرفي النهار is vocalized because it meets a following still consonant; still consonants are usually given kasra, as in صاحبي السجن.

AKHFASH:v1p391/r4.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p391/r4.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p391/r4.claim: زلفا is a plural of زلفة, with زلفات and زلف also used as plural forms.

TAB-FULL:v12p602/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r1.claim: The command is to pray at the two ends of the day, morning and evening; all interpreters agree that the morning prayer is Fajr but differ over the evening prayer.

TAB-FULL:v12p602/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r2.claim: Mujahid identifies the prayers as Fajr and the afternoon prayers, Zuhr and ʿAsr.

TAB-FULL:v12p602/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r3.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r3.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb identifies the ends as Fajr, Zuhr, and ʿAsr.

TAB-FULL:v12p602/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the two end-of-day prayers are the morning prayer and Maghrib.

TAB-FULL:v12p602/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r5.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r5.claim: Al-Hasan likewise identifies the prayers as Fajr and Maghrib.

TAB-FULL:v12p602/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r6.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r6.claim: Ibn Zayd says the prayers are morning and Maghrib.

TAB-FULL:v12p602/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r7.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v12p602/r7.claim: Al-Dahhak identifies the two prayers as Fajr and ʿAsr.

TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r1.claim: Al-Ṭabarī links the night phrase to the portion of night after which the ʿIsha prayer is performed.

TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r2.claim: Some Medinan readers pronounce both letters with ḍamma, while some Meccan readers use a silent lam.

TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r3.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the plural reading zulafan, with ḍamma on zay and fatḥa on lam, as the plural of zulfa; the ʿIsha prayer occurs after portions of night, matching the verse.

TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r4.claim: Mujahid, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn Zayd are cited as taking the night periods to mean the ʿIsha prayer alone.

TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r5.speaker: بعضهم
TAB-FULL:v12p606#2/r5.claim: Another group says the night periods refer to both Maghrib and ʿIsha; the report list continues in the next segment.

TAB-FULL:v12p606/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p606/r1.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
TAB-FULL:v12p606/r1.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Hasan, and Qatada are reported as identifying the prayers at the two ends as Fajr and ʿAsr.

TAB-FULL:v12p606/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p606/r2.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v12p606/r2.claim: Al-Hasan is separately reported as naming the morning and ʿAsr prayers.

TAB-FULL:v12p606/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p606/r3.speaker: بعضهم
TAB-FULL:v12p606/r3.claim: Some say the two ends are Zuhr and ʿAsr, while the night periods include Maghrib, ʿIsha, and Fajr.

TAB-FULL:v12p606/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p606/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p606/r4.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers Ibn ʿAbbas's pairing of Fajr and Maghrib: since everyone agrees one end is Fajr before sunrise, the other should be Maghrib after sunset; Zuhr and ʿAsr both fall in the day's latter half, not opposite ends.

TAB-FULL:v12p606/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p606/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p606/r5.claim: Al-Ṭabarī rejects the Zuhr-and-ʿAsr proposal because Zuhr follows midday and is in the second half of the day, so it cannot be the first endpoint while ʿAsr is the other.

TAB-FULL:v12p610/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p610/r1.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v12p610/r1.claim: Al-Hasan says the night periods are the two prayers, Maghrib and ʿIsha; the report attributes the same wording to the Prophet.

TAB-FULL:v12p610/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p610/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v12p610/r2.claim: Mujahid and other interpreters are reported as identifying the night prayers as Maghrib and ʿIsha.

TAB-FULL:v12p610/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p610/r3.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v12p610/r3.claim: Al-Hasan links prayer times to 17:78, naming dawn and ʿAsr at the day ends and Maghrib and ʿIsha as the night periods.

TAB-FULL:v12p611/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p611/r1.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
TAB-FULL:v12p611/r1.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Hasan, and al-Dahhak are among the authorities identifying the night periods as Maghrib and ʿIsha.

TAB-FULL:v12p612/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p612/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p612/r1.claim: Good deeds mean turning back to obedience and doing what pleases God; these acts remove the sins of disobedience and expiate transgressions.

TAB-FULL:v12p612/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p612/r2.speaker: كعب، محمد بن كعب القرظي، ابن عباس، مجاهد، الحسن، الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v12p612/r2.claim: A number of early authorities identify the good deeds in this verse as the five obligatory prayers; Kaʿb compares them to water washing away dirt.

TAB-FULL:v12p613/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p613/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v12p613/r1.claim: Ibn Masʿud identifies the good deeds as the five daily prayers.

TAB-FULL:v12p613/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p613/r2.speaker: سلمان
TAB-FULL:v12p613/r2.claim: Salman says the five prayers wash sins away like water removes dirt, as the Prophet's teaching illustrated.

TAB-FULL:v12p613/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p613/r3.speaker: النبي
TAB-FULL:v12p613/r3.claim: A report from the Prophet says the prayers serve as expiations for what occurs between them and cites this verse.

TAB-FULL:v12p613/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p613/r4.speaker: النبي
TAB-FULL:v12p613/r4.claim: The Prophet tells Salman that a Muslim who performs ablution well and prays the five prayers has sins fall away like leaves shaken from a dry branch, then recites this verse.

TAB-FULL:v12p616/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p616/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p616/r1.claim: Zulafan are night hours; zulfa can mean an hour, station, or nearness. Muzdalifa was said to derive from being a station after Arafat or from Adam approaching Eve there.

TAB-FULL:v12p616/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p616/r2.speaker: النبي
TAB-FULL:v12p616/r2.claim: Uthman reports the Prophet taught that the five daily prayers, with ablution and prayer, expiate sins between prayer times.

TAB-FULL:v12p616/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p616/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v12p616/r3.claim: Mujahid identifies the good deeds that erase sins as saying tasbih, praise, the testimony of faith, and takbir.

TAB-FULL:v12p616/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p616/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p616/r4.claim: Al-Tabari prefers the five prayers, citing sound, recurrent prophetic reports and the verse's immediate context of the command to establish prayer.

TAB-FULL:v12p618/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p618/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p618/r1.claim: The verse is a reminder for people who recall God's promise and hope for reward, and fear His warning; sealed hearts neither answer nor heed admonition.

TAB-FULL:v12p618/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p618/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v12p618/r2.claim: Ibn Masud reports a man confessed to an improper encounter short of intercourse; the Prophet recited the verse and said its lesson applied to everyone, not only the man.

TAB-FULL:v12p620/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p620/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v12p620/r1.claim: In another report, a man described touching and kissing a woman without intercourse; after the verse was recited, the Prophet answered that its guidance was general.

TAB-FULL:v12p620/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p620/r2.speaker: إبراهيم
TAB-FULL:v12p620/r2.claim: Ibrahim reports that the man was identified as an Ansari named Flan ibn Muattib and that the verse was revealed after his confession of an encounter short of intercourse.

TAB-FULL:v12p624#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p624#2/r1.speaker: أبو أمامة
TAB-FULL:v12p624#2/r1.claim: Abu Umama reports that a man seeking punishment was told that completing ablution and prayer with the Prophet cleansed his sin as at birth; the verse was then revealed.

TAB-FULL:v12p624#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p624#2/r2.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
TAB-FULL:v12p624#2/r2.claim: Muadh reports the Prophet told a man who confessed to forbidden contact to make a thorough ablution and pray, then said the verse applied generally to Muslims.

TAB-FULL:v12p624/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p624/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v12p624/r1.claim: A report from Ibn Masud says a man committed an act short of adultery; the verse was revealed, and the Prophet said it benefits anyone among his community who acts on it.

TAB-FULL:v12p624/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p624/r2.speaker: سلمان
TAB-FULL:v12p624/r2.claim: Salman reports that the Prophet compared sins falling away through excellent ablution to dry leaves falling from a branch, then recited the verse.

TAB-FULL:v12p624/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p624/r3.speaker: معاذ
TAB-FULL:v12p624/r3.claim: Muadh reports that after a man confessed to an encounter short of intercourse, the Prophet instructed him to perform ablution and pray, and said the instruction was general to believers.

TAB-FULL:v12p626#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p626#2/r1.speaker: سليمان التيمي
TAB-FULL:v12p626#2/r1.claim: Sulayman al-Taymi reports a man struck a woman's buttock, sought counsel from Abu Bakr and Umar, and received no answer from the Prophet until this verse came down.

TAB-FULL:v12p626#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p626#2/r2.speaker: عطاء
TAB-FULL:v12p626#2/r2.claim: Ata identifies the commanded prayers as the obligatory prayers in a report about a flour seller who kissed a woman and then sought guidance from Umar, Abu Bakr, and the Prophet.

TAB-FULL:v12p626#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p626#2/r3.speaker: يزيد بن رومان
TAB-FULL:v12p626#2/r3.claim: Yazid ibn Ruman reports a man of Banu Ghanm kissed a woman and placed his hand on her backside; after the verse was revealed, the man kept remembering its warning.

TAB-FULL:v12p626/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p626/r1.speaker: أبو اليسر
TAB-FULL:v12p626/r1.claim: Abu al-Yusr reports kissing a woman who came to buy dates; after consulting Abu Bakr and confessing to the Prophet, Gabriel brought the verse, which the Prophet said was for everyone.

TAB-FULL:v12p626/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p626/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v12p626/r2.claim: Qatada reports that a man who kissed a woman came to the Prophet saying he was ruined, and the verse was revealed in response.

ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r2.claim: The two ends of the day are morning and evening, specifically dawn, noon, and afternoon prayers; zulaf is near the beginning of night and refers to Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ.

ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r3.claim: Zulafan may also be read with ḍamma on zāy and lām; it is an adverbial plural of zulfa.

ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r4.claim: These prayers expiate the sins committed between them, confirming the report that prayers erase sins.

ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p82/r5.claim: Zulf is a plural of zulfa, or may be a plural like qarīb/qurb; he prefers the plural analysis and knows no use of zalīf for night.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r1.claim: The two ends of the day are the Maghrib and dawn prayers.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r2.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r2.claim: The ends of the day are morning, noon, and afternoon; Muhammad ibn Ka'b is also reported to hold this view.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas favored delaying the night prayer and recited “zulfan min al-layl.”

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r4.claim: The night intervals refer to the voluntary night prayer.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r5.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r5.claim: The two night intervals are Maghrib and Isha; Muhammad ibn Ka'b is also reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r6.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r6.claim: The two ends of the day mean Fajr and Isha.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r7.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r7.claim: A man who had kissed a woman asked the Prophet about expiation; the verse was revealed, and the Prophet said it applies to anyone in his community who acts likewise.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r8.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2091#2/r8.claim: A man said he had done everything with a woman except intercourse, and the verse was revealed.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r1.speaker: عثمان بن عفان
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r1.claim: A report from the Prophet says each obligatory prayer expiates sins committed since the preceding prayer; these prayers are the good deeds that erase sins.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r2.speaker: عطاء بن دينار
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r2.claim: Tasbih, praise of God, the declaration of divine unity, and the declaration of reliance on God are good deeds and the enduring righteous deeds.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r3.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r3.claim: Meet old sins with recent good deeds; Hasan finds confirmation in the verse that good deeds erase sins.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r4.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r4.claim: A servant is not among those who remember God abundantly until remembering him while standing, sitting, and lying down.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r5.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2092/r5.claim: Those who remember God in prosperity and adversity, hardship and ease, health and affliction are the people reminded by the verse.

NAHHAS:v2p306/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p306/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p306/r2.claim: طرفي النهار is a time adverb; readings vary on زلفا; حسنات may mean prayers, while repentance removes sins.

THALABI:v5p193/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p193/r1.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
THALABI:v5p193/r1.claim: Most commentators identify the good deeds that erase sins with the five daily prayers.

THALABI:v5p193/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p193/r2.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v5p193/r2.claim: Mujahid says the good deeds are saying glorification, praise, the testimony of divine unity, and God’s greatness.

THALABI:v5p193/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p193/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p193/r3.claim: The verse was revealed about Abu al-Yusr, a date seller who embraced and kissed a woman he had lured home, stopped when she reminded him of God, then confessed to the Prophet.

THALABI:v5p193/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p193/r4.speaker: النبي
THALABI:v5p193/r4.claim: After Gabriel brought the verse following the afternoon prayer, the Prophet told Abu al-Yusr that the prayer expiated his act; when Umar asked if this applied only to him, the Prophet said it applied to everyone.

THALABI:v5p193/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p193/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p193/r5.claim: The phrase that follows may point back to what was just mentioned, or alternatively to the Quran as a reminder for those who remember.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r1.claim: Everyone agrees the first edge of day is the dawn prayer; the second edge means noon and afternoon prayers (Mujahid), afternoon alone (Hasan), or sunset prayer (Ibn Abbas).

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r10.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r10.claim: The Prophet initially gave no reply, then summoned the man and recited the verse; when Umar asked whether it was only for him, the Prophet said it was for everyone.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r11.speaker: أبو موسى طمحان
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r11.claim: Abu Musa Tahman identifies the man as Abu al-Yusr al-Ansari; Ibn Abis calls him Amr ibn Ghaziya, and Muqatil calls him Amir ibn Qays, all Ansaris.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r2.claim: Zulaf is the plural of zulfa, a station or degree, meaning hours or periods of night; Muzdalifa is named as a stop after Arafat or because Adam drew near to Eve there.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r3.claim: The phrase may denote the late evening prayer (Ibn Abbas and Mujahid) or sunset and evening prayers (al-Dahhak and al-Hasan, who transmit it from the Prophet).

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Masud, and al-Dahhak interpret the good deeds as the five daily prayers.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r5.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r5.claim: Mujahid says good deeds are the phrases Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest; Ata calls them the enduring good works.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r6.claim: Other readings say accepted good deeds erase forgiven sins, or the reward of obedience removes the punishment of sins.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r7.speaker: الكلبي
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r7.claim: Al-Kalbi says the verse is a reminder or repentance for those who repent; another view makes it an admonition for those who heed.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r8.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r8.claim: The Prophet says to follow a bad deed with a good deed and it will erase it.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r9.speaker: ابن مسعود
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p508/r9.claim: Al-Aswad reports Ibn Masud's account of a man who had sexual contact short of intercourse with a woman near Medina and asked the Prophet for judgment; Umar said God had concealed him and he should have concealed himself.

QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r4.claim: Good deeds granted by God erase the servant’s sins; nearness, remorse, tears, and repentance are among the deeds that erase different faults.

QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r5.claim: Seeking forgiveness erases both disobedience and persistence in sin; divine solicitude erases wrongdoing.

QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r6.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r6.claim: Kindness toward fellow believers erases resentment, and generosity erases the wrongs of servants.

QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r7.claim: Good opinion erases their ill opinion of you; divine favor erases the belief that one’s obedience is self-earned.

QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r8.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p61/r8.claim: Truthfulness erases self-admiration, and sincerity erases ostentation.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r1.speaker: عامة المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r1.claim: The verse followed a man's question about sexual contact short of intercourse; the Prophet told him to perform ablution and pray, then said the ruling applies to everyone.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r2.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ's report, the two ends of the day are dawn, noon, and afternoon prayers.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r3.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r3.claim: Mujāhid, in the report of Manṣūr, identifies the prayers at the two ends as dawn, noon, and afternoon.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r4.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r4.claim: Al-Zajjāj identifies the day-end prayers as dawn, noon, and afternoon.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r5.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r5.claim: Muqātil adds the sunset prayer, assigning dawn and noon to one end and afternoon and sunset to the other.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r6.claim: The correct view is al-Zajjāj's: dawn is one end, noon and afternoon the other, while sunset belongs to the night.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r7.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid identifies the ends as dawn and sunset; al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd agree.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p578#2/r8.claim: The wording's apparent sense supports dawn and sunset; noon and afternoon are omitted because their place in daytime prayer is obvious and they are specified in 17:78.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r1.claim: The five daily prayers expiate the sins between them, provided major sins are avoided.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r2.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r2.claim: Through Layth, Mujāhid says the good deeds are the devotional phrases “Glory be to God,” praise, the testimony of faith, and takbīr.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r3.claim: ذلك is used in the sense of هذا: “this is an admonition.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r4.claim: Another interpretation takes ذلك ذكرى to mean that the Quran is an admonition for whoever remembers it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r5.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r5.claim: ذكرى is a verbal noun ending in feminine alif, patterned like العدوى and الدعوى, or like شورى; the text also discusses its plural and the variant ذِكر.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r6.speaker: سيبويه
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p582/r6.claim: Sībawayh records the form الذكر with dāl; Ibn Muqbil's line uses that form, which resembles words such as تقوى and تقية.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r1.claim: “The two ends of day” are the morning and sunset prayers, while the early portions of night mean the ʿishāʾ prayer near nightfall.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r2.claim: Another interpretation counts the ends of day as dawn, noon, and afternoon prayers, with sunset and night prayers among the early night prayers.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r3.claim: The five prayers expiate sins committed between them when major sins are avoided.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:114-116/r4.claim: This is an admonition for people who remember and take heed.

JISHUMI:v5p3576/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3576/r6.speaker: أبو مسلم
JISHUMI:v5p3576/r6.claim: Zulfā means closeness in rank; its plural appears in the name Muzdalifa and in the phrase that Paradise is brought near, while Abū Muslim also glosses it as successive time periods.

JISHUMI:v5p3576/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3576/r9.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3576/r9.claim: One occasion report concerns an Anṣārī date seller who lured a woman into his home and embraced her; she reminded him to fear God, he stopped and regretted it, and after he confessed, the Prophet said his prayer expiated it. ʿUmar asked whether this applied to him alone or everyone, and the Prophet answered everyone.

JISHUMI:v5p3579/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r1.speaker: أبو علي
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r1.claim: Abū ʿAlī's second interpretation is that repentance expiates major sins; the author says God intended both interpretations under discussion.

JISHUMI:v5p3579/r12.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r12.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r12.claim: Establishing prayer entails prayer in the specified times and establishes the times in general; the Prophet explained their details.

JISHUMI:v5p3579/r13.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r13.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r13.claim: The soundest account is Abū ʿAlī's: obedience removes sin through repentance; the claim cannot apply to every good deed, since unbelievers perform many good deeds without their sins being erased.

JISHUMI:v5p3579/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r2.claim: Another view says good deeds mean all good actions by the Prophet and believers, while sins mean all evil deeds by the polytheists; the verse promises victory for the Prophet and dominance of his religion.

JISHUMI:v5p3579/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r3.speaker: أبو مسلم
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r3.claim: Abū Muslim links the promise of good overcoming evil to the statement that truth is hurled against falsehood and crushes it.

JISHUMI:v5p3579/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r4.speaker: أبو مسلم
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r4.claim: Abū Muslim says the reminder makes believers firm in their religion.

JISHUMI:v5p3579/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r5.speaker: الأصم
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r5.claim: Al-Aṣamm says prayer reminds people of their sins, leading them to repent and avoid evil, as in the statement that prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing.

JISHUMI:v5p3579/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3579/r6.claim: Other explanations take ذلك as the Qur'an or as the promise itself being a reminder.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r1.claim: One reading of the day’s two ends is dawn and evening, meaning the dawn and sunset prayers; Mujahid includes dawn, noon, and afternoon, with sunset and night prayers as the night’s portions.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r2.speaker: مقاتل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r2.claim: Muqatil assigns dawn and noon prayer to one end of the day, afternoon and sunset to the other, and night prayer to the night’s portions.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r3.speaker: الحسن
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r3.claim: Al-Hasan takes the two ends as dawn and afternoon prayers, and the night portions as sunset and night prayers.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the ends as morning and evening, meaning dawn and sunset prayers.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p204/r5.claim: The night portions are its hours, each called a zulfa; Abu Jafar reads زلفا with a damma on the lam.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p205/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p205/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p205/r1.claim: “That” points either to what was just described or to the Quran; it is a reminder for those who remember.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r1.claim: The two ends of the day are morning and evening: dawn is the morning prayer, noon and afternoon are the evening prayers, and the night intervals are sunset and night prayers.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r2.claim: The accusative of the two ends is adverbial because the words are annexed to times; the annexed term takes the syntactic status of its complement.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r3.claim: He records forms with damma, quiescent lām, and the form zu lfā; the last means a near interval of night, as does qurbā.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r4.claim: On another parsing, the night intervals are prayers by which one draws near to God, so the phrase coordinates with prayer.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r5.claim: One explanation is that acts of obedience expiate minor sins.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r6.claim: A prophetic report says one prayer expiates what lies between it and the next, provided major sins are avoided.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r7.claim: A second explanation is that good deeds act as a moral prompting that helps people leave sins; he links this to reciting scripture.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p410/r8.claim: The verse is reported to have followed the repentance of Abu al-Yusr ʿAmr ibn Ghaziyya after he embraced and kissed a woman, then confessed to the Prophet.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p411/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p411/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p411/r1.claim: A report says Abu Bakr and ʿUmar each advised the penitent to conceal the matter and repent; when ʿUmar asked whether the verse applied only to him, the Prophet said it was for everyone.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p411/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p411/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p411/r2.claim: Another prophetic report instructs him to perform ablution well and pray two rakʿas, then cites the verse about good deeds removing sins.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p411/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p411/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p411/r3.claim: The demonstrative refers to the command to remain upright and what follows it; this is an admonition for those who take admonition.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r1.speaker: جمهور المتأولين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r1.claim: Most early interpreters take the good deeds that erase sins as the five prayers; Uthman invoked this verse while performing ablution, and this is Malik's interpretation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r2.claim: Mujahid says the good deeds are a person's repeated glorification, praise, profession of divine unity, and magnification of God.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r3.claim: These are examples of good deeds; the verse's wording is general for good deeds but specific to lesser sins in light of the Prophetic phrase 'if major sins are avoided.'

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r4.claim: A report says the verse came after an Ansari man—identified as Abu al-Yusr ibn Amr or as Abbad—met a woman alone and kissed and fondled her without intercourse; after he told Umar and Abu Bakr, he confessed to the Prophet, who recited the verse. Muadh asked if it was only for him; the Prophet said it was for everyone. Another report says the verse predated the incident and was applied to him.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r5.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r5.claim: The Prophet said Friday to Friday, the five prayers, and Ramadan to Ramadan expiate what lies between them if major sins are avoided.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r6.speaker: جمهور أهل السنة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r6.claim: Most Sunni scholars make avoiding major sins a condition of the entire promise: without it, the named acts do not expiate lesser sins.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r7.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p212#2/r7.claim: Another group says major sins are the sins the acts do not erase; the condition preserves the hadith's broad wording while the acts still erase lesser sins.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p213/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p213/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p213/r1.claim: Ibn Atiyya adopts the second interpretation: the hadith about sins falling away with drops of water supports it, provided minor sins are repented of and not persisted in; he calls this the precise view of expert legal theorists. On the first interpretation, the verse applies only to those who avoid major sins.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p213/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p213/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p213/r2.claim: ذلك may refer to the prayers as a cause and setting for remembrance, to the claim that good deeds erase sins as encouragement toward good deeds, or to all the preceding commands and prohibitions, as al-Tabari explains.

TABRISI:11:113-116/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:113-116/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:113-116/r11.claim: طرفي النهار is a temporal accusative, with زلفا coordinated to it.

TABRISI:11:113-116/r18.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:113-116/r18.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:113-116/r18.claim: Establish prayer by completing its acts of bowing, prostration, and other obligations.

TABRISI:11:113-117/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:113-117/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:113-117/r1.claim: Al-Tabrisi reports from Abu Umama that a man confessed an offense and asked the Prophet to impose its legal penalty; the Prophet said prayer had brought forgiveness from God.

TABRISI:11:113-117/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:113-117/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:113-117/r2.claim: Al-Tabrisi transmits from al-Harith, from Ali, that after a man confessed, the Prophet called his well-performed prayer and ablution expiation for the sin.

TABRISI:11:113-117/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:113-117/r3.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABRISI:11:113-117/r3.claim: Al-Sadiq advises a visitor to account for each day and night because a noble angel records his public and hidden acts; he should neither dismiss a sin nor belittle a good deed.

TABRISI:11:113-117/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:113-117/r4.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABRISI:11:113-117/r4.claim: Al-Sadiq says a good deed can catch and remove even a great old sin forgotten by its doer, after it has been recorded, illustrating that good deeds erase sins.

TABRISI:11:113-117/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:113-117/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:113-117/r5.claim: Abu Hamza al-Thumali reports that Ali asked which Quranic verse gives the greatest hope; one person proposed a verse, but Ali said it was good, not the one he meant.

TABRISI:11:113-117/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:113-117/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:113-117/r6.claim: In the report from Abu Hamza al-Thumali, a second respondent cites the promise to forgive one who does evil or wrongs himself; Ali again says it is good but not the sought verse.

TABRISI:11:114#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114#2/r1.speaker: علي
TABRISI:11:114#2/r1.claim: Ali reports that the Prophet called the prayer command in this verse the most hopeful verse in the Book.

TABRISI:11:114#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114#2/r2.speaker: علي
TABRISI:11:114#2/r2.claim: The Prophet compares the five daily prayers to bathing five times in a river: prayer removes sins as washing removes bodily dirt.

TABRISI:11:114#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114#2/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:114#2/r3.claim: One interpretation is that persistence in good deeds leads a person to abandon evil deeds, as though the good deeds remove them.

TABRISI:11:114#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114#2/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:114#2/r4.claim: A second interpretation identifies the good deeds as repentance, which removes sins by cancelling their punishment; the author says there is no disagreement that repentance cancels punishment.

TABRISI:11:114#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114#2/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:114#2/r5.claim: The reminder is an admonition for whoever reflects on the teaching that good deeds remove evil deeds.

TABRISI:11:114/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:114/r1.claim: Other glosses say to perform prayer evenly or to keep performing it continuously.

TABRISI:11:114/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114/r2.speaker: ابن عباس، ابن زيد
TABRISI:11:114/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd identify the two ends of day as dawn and sunset prayers and the night intervals as the first hours of night, including the final evening prayer.

TABRISI:11:114/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114/r3.speaker: ابن عباس، ابن زيد
TABRISI:11:114/r3.claim: They say noon and afternoon prayers are omitted either because they are obviously daytime prayers or because they fall near the day's latter end after noon; 17:78 specifies the sun's decline, meaning noon, and this is the report from Abu Ja'far.

TABRISI:11:114/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114/r4.speaker: الزجاج، مجاهد، الضحاك، محمد بن كعب القرظي، الحسن
TABRISI:11:114/r4.claim: Al-Zajjaj, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, and Hasan take the day prayers as dawn, noon, and afternoon and the night prayers as sunset and the final evening prayer, since sunset belongs to night.

TABRISI:11:114/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114/r5.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:11:114/r5.claim: Hasan reports the Prophet's wording that Maghrib and Isha are the two night intervals called zulf.

TABRISI:11:114/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:114/r6.claim: A further view identifies the two ends as the dawn and afternoon prayers.

TABRISI:11:114/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114/r7.speaker: ابن عباس وأكثر المفسرين
TABRISI:11:114/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas and most commentators say the five daily prayers expiate sins committed between them, taking the definite good deeds as referring back to prayer.

TABRISI:11:114/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:114/r8.speaker: سلمان
TABRISI:11:114/r8.claim: Salman demonstrates a dry branch shedding leaves, then reports that the Prophet taught that good ablution and the five prayers shed a Muslim's sins like those leaves and recited this verse.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r1.speaker: علقمة والأسود عن ابن مسعود
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r1.claim: A man confessed to the Prophet that he had kissed, embraced, and fondled a woman in a garden without intercourse; after the Prophet fell silent, this verse was revealed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r10.speaker: الجمهور
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r10.claim: The first end of the day is the dawn prayer according to the majority; Ibn Jarir instead reports the noon prayer.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r2.speaker: عمر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r2.claim: In one report Umar asks whether the verse applies only to the man in the incident; the Prophet answers that it applies to everyone.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r3.claim: Another Ibn Masud report says a man told the Prophet he had kissed a woman, and the verse descended; the man asks if it is for him, and the Prophet says it is for whoever acts by it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r4.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r4.claim: Muadh reports a man described every unlawful intimacy short of intercourse; the Prophet told him to perform ablution well and pray, then the verse was revealed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r5.speaker: أبو صالح عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r5.claim: Abu Salih identifies the man as Amr ibn Ghaziya al-Ansari, a date seller who lured a customer by claiming better dates were at home.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r6.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r6.claim: Muqatil identifies the man as Abu Miqbal Amir ibn Qays al-Ansari.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r7.speaker: أحمد بن علي بن ثابت الخطيب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r7.claim: Al-Khatib identifies the man as Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn Amr al-Ansari.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r8.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r8.claim: The source gives three possible questioners asking whether the ruling was special: Abu al-Yusr, Muadh ibn Jabal, or Umar ibn al-Khattab.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r9.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p165#3/r9.claim: “Establish prayer” means perform its bowing and prostration completely.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r1.speaker: ابن عباس وابن زيد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd identify the second end of the day with the sunset prayer.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r2.speaker: قتادة والحسن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r2.claim: Qatada identifies the second end with the afternoon prayer; al-Hasan is reported to hold either this or the sunset view.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r3.speaker: مجاهد والقرظي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r3.claim: Mujahid and al-Qurazi identify the second end of the day with both noon and afternoon prayers.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r4.speaker: الضحاك
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r4.claim: Al-Dahhak is reported to accept all three interpretations of the second end of the day.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r5.claim: Abu Ja'far and Shayba read zulafan with a ḍamma on the lām.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r6.speaker: أبو عبيدة والعجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r6.claim: Abu Ubayda explains zulaf as hours or stages, singular zulfa; al-Ajjaj's poem uses it for successive nighttime intervals.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r7.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r7.claim: Ibn Qutayba connects the term with drawing near: azlafani means brought me close, and mazalif are stages or steps.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r8.speaker: ابن عباس وابن زيد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r8.claim: One interpretation identifies the nighttime intervals as the late evening prayer, reported from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Mujahid and adopted by Ibn Zayd.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r9.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وقتادة ومقاتل والزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p167/r9.claim: The other interpretation identifies them as sunset and night prayers; reports and named authorities support this view.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس وابن المسيب ومسروق ومجاهد والقرظي والضحاك ومقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r1.claim: These authorities identify the good deeds that erase sins as the five daily prayers.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r2.speaker: منصور عن مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r2.claim: Mansur transmits from Mujahid that the good deeds are saying “Glory be to God, praise be to God, no deity but God, and God is greatest.”

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r3.claim: The author prefers the five-prayer interpretation because most authorities hold it and a connected Prophetic report supports it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r4.speaker: عثمان عن رسول الله
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r4.claim: Uthman reports that ablution followed by each prayer expiates sins committed since the preceding prayer; these prayers are the good deeds that erase sins.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r5.speaker: المفسرون
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r5.claim: The commentators identify the sins erased here as minor sins.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r6.speaker: معاذ بن جبل عن النبي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p168/r6.claim: Muadh reports the Prophet's advice to fear God, follow a bad deed with a good one to erase it, and treat people well.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p169/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p169/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p169/r1.claim: “That” may refer to the Qur'an, the establishment of prayer, or all preceding counsel: steadfastness, avoiding transgression and unjust rulers, and prayer.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p169/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p169/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p169/r2.claim: The word “reminder” is interpreted either as repentance or as admonition.

RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r1.claim: The command to pray follows the command to be steadfast, indicating that prayer is the greatest act of worship after faith.

RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r2.speaker: الخوارج
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r2.claim: The Khārijites argue that only dawn and nightfall prayers are obligatory because they fall at the two day edges; they treat the night phrase as an adjective of the day edges.

RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r3.speaker: الخوارج
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r3.claim: They also argue that the two prayers expiate every sin, even omission of the other prayers, by the statement that good deeds remove evil deeds.

RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r4.claim: Rāzī rejects the Khārijite claim that only two prayers are required as contrary to the community's consensus.

RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r5.claim: The closest reading of the day edges is dawn and afternoon prayer: sunrise marks one edge, sunset the other, while sunset prayer is included among the night intervals.

RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r6.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v18p58#2/r6.claim: Rāzī says the verse supports Abū Ḥanīfa's preference to perform dawn prayer later in its time and afternoon prayer later, near sunset.

RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the five prayers expiate lesser sins, provided major sins are avoided.

RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r2.claim: Mujāhid identifies good deeds as the devotional phrases “Glory be to God,” praise, the declaration of unity, and magnifying God.

RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r3.claim: Those arguing sin cannot harm a believer infer that faith, the greatest good deed, removes unbelief and therefore lesser sins; at minimum it removes eternal punishment.

RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p59#2/r4.claim: The demonstrative “that” refers to the passage from “be steadfast” onward and serves as admonition for those who reflect and seek guidance.

RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r1.claim: Because zulf is a plural with minimum three, Rāzī infers three night prayer intervals; since Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ account for two, he argues witr is obligatory for the Prophet and, by 34:20, everyone.

RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r2.claim: The wording about glorification before sunrise and before sunset in 20:130 likewise refers to Fajr and ʿAṣr; the night portions parallel zulf.

RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r3.claim: A report says a man who had intimate contact with a forbidden woman short of intercourse asked the Prophet what to do; he prescribed good ablution and prayer, then this verse was revealed and he said the ruling applied to everyone.

RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r4.speaker: الليث
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r4.claim: Al-Layth defines a zulfah as a portion at the beginning of the night and zulf as its plural.

RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r5.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r5.claim: Al-Wāḥidī derives the term from closeness: azlaftuhu fa-izdalafa means I brought him near and he approached.

RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r6.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
RAZI-FULL:v18p59/r6.claim: Al-Kashshāf notes readings زلفا with two ḍammas, with a still lām, and زلفى; it explains زلف as a plural of zulfah and zulfā as its equivalent.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r1.speaker: جمهور المتأولين من الصحابة والتابعين
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r1.claim: Most early interpreters identify the good deeds that erase sins as the five daily prayers.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r10.claim: On the view that a zulfah is the first hour after sunset, the night portion means the nightfall prayer, according to Ibn Abbas.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r11.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r11.claim: Al-Hasan interprets the night portion as sunset and nightfall prayers.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r12.speaker: الأخفش
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r12.claim: Al-Akhfash says the phrase means night prayer without specifying which prayer.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r2.claim: Mujahid says the good deeds include saying glory and praise to God and affirming His oneness and greatness; Ibn Atiyya treats this as an example.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r3.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r3.claim: Ibn Atiyya says Mujahid's list is illustrative; the wording is general about good deeds but specific to lesser sins, as long as major sins are avoided.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r4.claim: The occasion of revelation supports the majority: an Ansari, identified by some as Abu al-Yusr ibn Amr and by others as Abbad, had an intimate encounter short of intercourse.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r5.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r5.claim: In a Tirmidhi report from Abdullah, a man confesses to intimacy short of intercourse; after reciting the verse, the Prophet says it applies to everyone, not only that man. Tirmidhi grades it hasan sahih.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r6.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r6.claim: Another Tirmidhi report from Ibn Masud concerns a forbidden kiss; the Prophet says the verse applies to the questioner and whoever acts on it from his community, and Tirmidhi grades the report hasan sahih.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r7.speaker: مجاهد وابن محيصن
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r7.claim: Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin also read زلفى, like قربى.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r8.claim: The remaining readers use زلف with an open lām, like غرفة and غرف.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r9.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#2/r9.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says zalaf means hours and zulfah is its singular.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r1.speaker: أبو اليسر
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r1.claim: Abu al-Yusr recounts kissing a woman who came to buy dates; after he confessed to Abu Bakr and Umar, he told the Prophet, feared Hell, and received the verse. The Prophet said it was for everyone; al-Tirmidhi calls this report hasan gharib and notes Qays ibn al-Rabi was weakened.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r2.claim: An alternative report says the Prophet turned away from the man, then after the afternoon prayer Gabriel brought the verse; the Prophet asked whether he had prayed with them and called the prayer an expiation.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r3.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r3.claim: Another report says the Prophet told the man to perform four cycles of prayer after reciting the verse.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r4.claim: Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim transmits from Ibn Abbas that no good deed answers and reaches an old sin more quickly than a recent good deed.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r5.claim: The verse and reports show that an unlawful kiss or touch does not incur the fixed penalty.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r6.speaker: ابن المنذر
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#3/r6.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir is said to choose that no fixed penalty or discretionary punishment applies when a man and woman are found in one garment, using this report as evidence.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r1.claim: The Quran names prayer's postures and recitation, but gives its outline; the Prophet explained times, units, required conditions, sunnah, and virtues, as commanded in 16:44.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r2.claim: The Prophet said, Pray as you have seen me pray; the community transmitted his explanation broadly, and he completed what people need before his death.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r3.claim: The completed religion and clarified path are affirmed by the verse declaring God's favor and religion complete.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114#4/r4.claim: The Quran is an admonition and call to repentance for those who take heed; they are singled out because they benefit, and dhikra is a verbal noun with feminine ending.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r1.speaker: جمهور أهل التأويل
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r1.claim: Interpreters agree that prayer here means the obligatory prayers; prayer follows faith and is a refuge in hardship, as the Prophet turned to it when troubled.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r10.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r10.claim: Ibn Atiyya objects that sunset belongs to the night, so cannot be an end of daytime.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r11.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r11.claim: Ibn al-Arabi mocks al-Tabari's pairing as making the two ends of the day dawn and sunset, which he calls the ends of night.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r12.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r12.claim: Al-Tabari replies that since all agree one end is dawn and no other pairing is agreed, the other end must be sunset.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r13.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r13.claim: The author calls Ibn al-Arabi's rebuttal excessive: Mujahid supports dawn, and the rule that deliberate eating or intercourse after dawn invalidates the fast confirms dawn is daytime, though the sunset objection remains.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r14.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r14.claim: Zulaf means successive near hours; al-Muzdalifa is named for being a stop near Mecca after Arafat.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r15.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r15.speaker: ابن قعقاع وابن أبي إسحاق وغيرهما
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r15.claim: These readers use زلف with a damma on the lām, either a plural of zalif or a dialectal singular zulfah.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r16.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r16.speaker: ابن محيصن
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r16.claim: Ibn Muhaysin reads زلف with a silent lām, treating it as the singular zulfah used collectively.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r2.speaker: شيوخ الصوفية
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r2.claim: Sufi authorities say the verse commands filling all time with worship, obligatory and voluntary.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r3.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r3.claim: Ibn al-Arabi rejects the all-time worship reading: the command covers obligations, while litanies and recommended prayers have bounded times and other voluntary acts rotate rather than fill every hour.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r4.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r4.claim: Mujahid identifies the two ends of the day as dawn at the first end and noon plus afternoon prayers at the second; Ibn Atiyya chooses this view.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r5.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan identify the two ends as dawn and sunset; al-Hasan also reports a second end consisting of the afternoon prayer alone, as do Qatada and al-Dahhak.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r6.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r6.claim: Another view identifies the ends as noon and afternoon; its account of the night hours includes sunset, nightfall, and dawn, apparently tracking loud recitation.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r7.speaker: الماوردي
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r7.claim: Al-Mawardi reports agreement that the first end of the day is the dawn prayer.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r8.claim: The author says this reported agreement is qualified by the preceding view that does not place dawn at that end.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r9.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:11:114/r9.claim: Al-Tabari prefers dawn and sunset as the two ends, arguing that everyone agrees dawn is one end and sunset must be the other.

BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r1.claim: The two ends of the day are morning and evening: dawn prayer is the first prayer near daytime, while the evening prayer may mean afternoon or noon and afternoon; the nearby night prayers are sunset and night prayer.

BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r2.claim: Zulafan are hours near the day, a plural of zulfa; readings include zuluf, zuluf, and zulfa, with the latter meaning one near period.

BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r3.claim: Good deeds erase sins, and prayer from one prayer to the next expiates what lies between them if major sins are avoided.

BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r4.speaker: رجل
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r4.claim: A man told the Prophet that he had done something with a woman but had not had intercourse; this verse was revealed.

BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:114/r5.claim: The phrase 'that is a reminder' may refer to steadfastness and what follows or to the Qur'an; it is an admonition for those who take heed.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r1.claim: The two ends of day mean morning and evening: dawn prayer, and afternoon prayer after noon, which includes noon and afternoon; the night periods near day's end are sunset and night prayers.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r2.claim: The accusative dual 'ends' functions adverbially because the words are annexed to times, as in phrases giving a whole or half day.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r3.claim: The five prayers expiate sins committed between them; alternatively good deeds generally erase sins, as in the prophetic instruction to follow an evil deed with a good one.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r4.claim: The Prophet also recommends saying 'Glory be to God, praise belongs to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest.'

NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r5.claim: That may refer to the instruction beginning 'remain steadfast' and what follows, or to the Qur'an as admonition for those who take heed.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r6.claim: The verse was revealed about ʿAmr ibn Ghaziyya al-Anṣārī, a date seller who entered a woman's home and kissed her, then repented; the Prophet said his joining the afternoon prayer expiated it, and that the rule applied to everyone.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r7.speaker: النبي
NASAFI-FULL:v2p175/r7.claim: The Prophet asks whether the man prayed the afternoon prayer with them, calls it an expiation, and says this applies to all people, not him alone.

QASHANI:11:114-115/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:11:114-115/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:11:114-115/r1.claim: The five senses distract the heart with bodily forms and veil it from divine presence; five prayers close those sensory doors, open the heart to God, focus attention, and admit light.

QASHANI:11:114-115/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:11:114-115/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:11:114-115/r2.claim: Prayer's incoming light removes the darkness and residue of sensory distractions, meaning that good deeds remove evil deeds.

QASHANI:11:114-115/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:11:114-115/r3.speaker: عليه السلام
QASHANI:11:114-115/r3.claim: A prophetic report says one prayer expiates what lies between it and the next, provided major sins are avoided.

QASHANI:11:114-115/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:11:114-115/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:11:114-115/r4.claim: Praying at both ends of the day lets gathered presence and light persist through other times and remove their fragmentation, sustaining continual prayer.

QASHANI:11:114-115/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:11:114-115/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:11:114-115/r5.claim: Natural powers dominate at night, drawing the soul to bodily management and sleep and away from spiritual perception; wakefulness and prayer refine and illuminate them.

QASHANI:11:114-115/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:11:114-115/r6.speaker: author
QASHANI:11:114-115/r6.claim: These prayer times and removal of sins remind those who remember their state of clarity, gathered attention, intimacy, and spiritual taste.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r1.speaker: الليث
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r1.claim: Al-Layth defines زلفة as a portion of the first part of night and gives زلف as its plural.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r2.speaker: ثعلب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r2.claim: Thaʿlab says زلف are the first hours of night and زلفة is singular.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r3.speaker: أبو عبيدة، والأخفش، وابن قتيبة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r3.claim: They gloss زلف as the hours and periods of night, each hour being a زلفة; al-Ajjaj's verse illustrates the word's repeated plural form.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p214/r4.claim: زلفة derives from nearness and approach, as shown by the related forms meaning to bring near and draw close.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r1.claim: A report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim says the verse was revealed after a man had relations with a non-maḥram woman short of intercourse.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r10.claim: A further view takes Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr as the boundaries and dawn, Maghrib, and ʿIshāʾ as night prayers, apparently grouping them by recitation aloud or quietly.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r2.claim: Another account says the verse predated the incident and the Prophet applied it to that man; when asked whether it was only for him, he said it was for everyone.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r3.claim: Addressing the Prophet directly in commands to do good, while directing prohibitions to the community, is a mark of eloquence.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r4.claim: The commanded prayer is the obligatory prayer; إقامة means maintaining it continuously, performing it fully, or performing it at its best times.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r5.claim: طرفي النهار is an adverbial accusative; because each طرف belongs to the thing it bounds, the apparent referents are dawn and afternoon.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r6.claim: The fasting rule that dawn belongs to daytime supports dawn as one boundary: deliberate eating or intercourse after dawn invalidates the fast and entails makeup and expiation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r7.speaker: الحسن وقتادة والضحاك
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r7.claim: They identify the two daytime prayers as dawn and ʿAṣr, and the night approaches as Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, leaving Ẓuhr outside this verse.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r8.speaker: مجاهد ومحمد بن كعب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r8.claim: They assign the first boundary to dawn and the second to Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr, with Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ at night; the passage says dawn is not included in this verse.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p221#2/r9.claim: They identify the boundaries as dawn and Maghrib and the night prayer as ʿIshāʾ, excluding Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r1.speaker: الطبري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r1.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers Ibn ʿAbbās’s dawn-and-Maghrib interpretation; Abū Ḥayyān objects that Maghrib belongs to night, so calling it a daytime boundary requires metaphor.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r10.claim: Hasanāt can mean all good deeds, especially obligatory prayers and Ramadan fasting; sayyiʾāt in this reading means minor sins, as supported by the sound report about avoiding major sins.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r11.speaker: جمهور المتأولين من الصحابة والتابعين
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r11.claim: Most early interpreters identify the good deeds specifically as the five prayers; Mālik adopts this interpretation, and ʿUthmān illustrates it while performing ablution.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r12.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r12.claim: Mujāhid interprets the good deeds as the formulas of remembrance: glorifying and praising God, proclaiming his oneness and greatness, and declaring reliance on him.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r13.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r13.claim: These interpretations should be understood as examples; the five prayers are the greatest deeds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r14.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r14.claim: Minor sins are erased only when one repents and does not persist in them, a position stated explicitly by the most discerning legal theorists.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r15.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r15.claim: Erasing sins means expiating minor sins, not making past acts cease to have happened.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r16.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r16.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r16.claim: Another explanation is that good deeds graciously help people leave sins rather than erase sins already committed, as prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r17.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r17.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r17.claim: The demonstrative ذلك most apparently points to the nearest command: establishing prayer at these times as a reminder for those who take heed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r18.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r18.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r18.claim: Other referents for ذلك are the news that good deeds erase sins, earlier commands and prohibitions, or the Qurʾān; al-Zamakhsharī gives the earlier counsel as his view and al-Ṭabarī points to this sūrah's commands.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes dawn as the morning prayer, Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr as afternoon prayers, and Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ as the night approaches.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r3.claim: Calling the period after noon ʿashiyy does not make Ẓuhr a boundary, since the command names the day's two boundaries rather than morning and afternoon.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r4.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r4.claim: The majority read zulafan with an open lām.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r5.speaker: طلحة وعيسى البصرة وابن أبي إسحاق وأبو جعفر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r5.claim: These readers use a damma on the lām, as though the word were a singular noun.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r6.speaker: ابن محيصن ومجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r6.claim: They read the lām quiescent; a further transmission from them has zulfa on the fuʿlā pattern, a feminine singular meaning a station or degree.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r7.claim: The plural readings treat the word as successive stations or as a collective noun; zulafā is equivalent to one zalfa.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r8.claim: The apparent syntax coordinates the night approaches with the two daytime boundaries as another bounded period.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r9.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p222/r9.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains zulaf as the part of the day near nightfall; another interpretation makes it night prayers of devotion and coordinates it with الصلاة instead.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r1.speaker: ثعلب
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r1.claim: Thaʿlab defines زلفة as the first hours of the night.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r2.speaker: الأخفش وابن قتيبة
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r2.claim: Al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutayba use زلف for the night hours generally, with every hour counting as a zulfa.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r3.speaker: العجاج
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r3.claim: Al-Ajjaj's verse uses زلفا زلفا for successive portions of night.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r4.claim: The root conveys nearness: أزلفه فازدلف means to bring near and draw close, also used in الشعراء 26:64 and the cited hadith.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r5.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r5.claim: Al-Raghib says zulfa can mean rank or favor, can euphemistically denote punishment like بشارة, and gives the related meanings of steps and the name Muzdalifa.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:114#2/r6.claim: من الليل is an adjective modifying زلفا.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r1.claim: طرفي النهار is an adverb governed by أقم; attaching it to الصلاة as the times when prayer occurs is weaker.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r2.claim: طرف is not inherently a temporal adverb, but acquires that case after إضافة to a time expression, as in أول النهار and نصف الليل.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r3.speaker: العامة
SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r3.claim: The common reading زلفا has zay with damma and lam with fatha, a plural of زلفة with a still lam.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r4.speaker: أبو جعفر وابن أبي إسحاق
SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r4.claim: Their doubled-vowel reading can be a plural of زلفة with vowel harmony, a singular on the pattern of عنق, or a plural of زليف.

SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:114/r5.speaker: مجاهد وابن محيصن
